fieldworkDocument.title: Measgaichte / Miscellaneous
fieldworkDocument.note: [NOTES: some notes added (most probably by K. D. MacDonald?). See below for details.]

item.description: superstitions. “Tha thu làn de na geaslagan.”
superstitious.
a long, untidy beard. “Bha réip air.” [NOTES: note added above ‘p’ in ‘réip’ – b.]
a stripy long skirt, characterised by striking colours, usually red, white and blue.
also a long skirt [cf. còta drògaid], usually wine coloured.
a flannel underskirt, usually scarlet coloured.
cable stitch in knitting. [NOTES: note added above ‘dual’ – dubhal.]
fern leaf pattern in knitting.
thistle pattern. [NOTES: corrected to ‘githeagan’.]
chalice. [NOTES: note added – cailis.]
mushroom.
this was a mode of measurement which involved putting the heel of one shoe next to the toe of the other foot. Distance was measured using this system.
informant uses this in the sense of trudging as in trudging your feet. [NOTES: corrected to ‘rudanadh’.]
“Latha Fheill Moire, mór ’s t-fhoghar, buain is ceangal” – this saying would be uttered on the 15th of August.
would be applied to a mischievous person, someone who was always in trouble. “Nach ’be tu an trùdhleach.”
similar in meaning to the above [i.e. trùdhleach (q.v.)].
a desire to give someone a ticking off due to having committed some trivial but annoying offence. [NOTES: ‘fhasg’ corrected to ‘fhàsg’.]
so called since traditionally, this day was expected to be sunny.
a group, e.g. of people. “’Se droch sheathd a tha sin.” [NOTES: note added above ‘seathd’ – seat.]
to force something on someone else.
to polish your shoes. [NOTES: corrected to ‘blacadh’.]
shoe polish. [NOTES: corrected to ‘bleicinn’.]
cabbage garden.
a name applied to cattle that came from Mull.
located in Roman Catholic chapels. Usually located beside the tabernacle. A red coloured glass cylinder with a candle burning inside at night.
a particular type of sail boat.
an unexpected visit from a group of people. [NOTES: ‘phraig’ corrected to ‘phràig’ and note added above ‘ph’ – f.]
bawling as in ‘ag éigheach ’sa …’. [NOTES: note added above ‘u’ in ‘blaudaireachd’ – bh.]
